title: ArrayList vs LinkedList: when to use each
shortTitle: When do you use ArrayList vs LinkedList?
keyPoints: ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array with O(1) random access and excellent CPU cache locality; it is the default choice for 95% of use cases
LinkedList is a doubly-linked list with O(1) add/remove at head and tail but O(n) random access due to node traversal
ArrayList uses ~4 bytes per element (object reference); LinkedList uses ~40 bytes per node (object header + item + prev + next)
Even for insert/remove in the middle, ArrayList often wins because System.arraycopy is a CPU-optimized memory move while LinkedList requires pointer chasing with cache misses
LinkedList's only real advantage is O(1) insert/remove at the current ListIterator position during traversal
For queue/stack behavior, use ArrayDeque instead of LinkedList because it is faster and uses less memory
Both are not thread-safe; use CopyOnWriteArrayList or Collections.synchronizedList() for concurrent access

s1_definition.oneliner: ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array with O(1) get and cache-friendly memory layout; LinkedList is a doubly-linked list with O(1) add/remove at the ends but O(n) random access. Use ArrayList as the default.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **ArrayList** stores elements in a contiguous `Object[]` array; `get(i)` is O(1) direct array access, `add()` at end is amortized O(1), but insert/remove in the middle is O(n) because elements must be shifted
- **LinkedList** stores each element in a `Node` object with `prev` and `next` pointers; addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast are O(1), but `get(i)` is O(n) because it must traverse nodes from head or tail
- In practice, ArrayList wins 95% of the time because CPU cache locality (contiguous memory) makes it faster even for operations where LinkedList has better theoretical complexity
- LinkedList implements both `List` and `Deque`; ArrayList implements only `List` and `RandomAccess`
s1_definition.analogy: ArrayList is like a bank's account ledger in a bound book with numbered pages. Finding account number 500 means flipping directly to page 500 – instant. Adding a new account at the end means writing on the next blank page – fast. But inserting an account in the middle means rewriting all subsequent pages to make room. LinkedList is like accounts written on sticky notes chained together. Adding or removing a note at either end is instant – just stick or unstick one note. But finding account number 500 means following the chain from note 1 to note 2 to note 3, all the way to note 500.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ArrayList (contiguous array)
  ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
  │  A  │  B  │  C  │  D  │  E  │     │     │
  └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
  get(2) → arr[2] → C  (O(1) direct access)
  add(0, X) → shift all right, then arr[0] = X  (O(n))

  LinkedList (doubly-linked nodes)
  first                                      last
    ↓                                          ↓
  ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐   ┌─────┐
  │  A  │⇄│  B  │⇄│  C  │⇄│  D  │⇄│  E  │
  └─────┘   └─────┘   └─────┘   └─────┘   └─────┘
  get(2) → A → B → C  (O(n) traversal)
  addFirst(X) → update first pointer  (O(1))

  Decision:
  Need get(index)?     → ArrayList
  Need queue/stack?    → ArrayDeque
  Need iterator insert? → LinkedList
  Default choice?      → ArrayList
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ArrayList is backed by a contiguous dynamic array. It gives you O(1) random access, excellent CPU cache locality, and compact memory usage at about 4 bytes per element. LinkedList wraps each element in a Node object scattered across the heap, giving O(1) add/remove at the ends but O(n) random access and about 40 bytes per element.

In practice, ArrayList wins 95% of the time. Even for operations where LinkedList has better theoretical complexity – like inserting at position zero – ArrayList's `System.arraycopy` (a CPU-optimized memory move) is often faster than LinkedList's pointer chasing through scattered heap nodes. The cache miss penalty dominates.

In the National Bank of India system, Rajesh uses ArrayList for the transaction history of account SAV2001 because he needs O(1) index access for pagination: "show me transactions 50 through 59." For the transaction processing queue, he uses ArrayDeque rather than LinkedList because ArrayDeque has the same O(1) offer/poll performance but with contiguous memory.

Remember one sentence: use ArrayList as your default, ArrayDeque for queue and stack behavior, and LinkedList only when you need O(1) insert/remove at the current ListIterator position during traversal.
